introParagraph: The capital of Romania, Bucharest, once a disorganised and rather oriental city, became, by the turn of the 20th century, a modern European city heavily inspired by French architecture and planning. This led to the city gaining the nickname of 'Paris of the East' or 'Little Paris'.
introParagraph2: During the Interwar period, Bucharest saw a flourishing of the arts and culture alongside great development in its economy and social life. In Interwar Romania, Bucharest set the standard and all of the latest fashion trends and technological advancements reached the capital first. From some of the most beautiful buildings and avenues, to the most chic parlors, entertaining cultural spots and newest movies, Bucharest had the best the country could offer.
introParagraph3: While the age of jazz and the likes of cabaret and charleston dancers have long departed from the streets of Bucharest and its Interwar charm has faded over time, archival images, magazines and other items from the era can still paint a picture of what once was in the capital of Romania. If you look closely, you can still find glimpses of its former glory today, so take a chance and explore Interwar Bucharest!
TransportMainText1: Bucharest's public transport company was initially exclusively formed as a tram transit company (known as 'Societatea Română de Tramvaiuri') in 1871.
TransportMainText2: In 1894 the first electric trams were introduced, alongside the existing horse-drawn ones, and in 1909 following a public transit law, the company becomes S.T.B ('Societatea comunală pentru construcțiunea și exploatarea tramvaielor în orașul București' shortened as 'Societatea de Tramvaie București').
TransportMainText3: In the early 1920s the first commercial buses enter sevice and by 1929 the last horse-drawn trams are retired. In 1936 S.T.B officially becomes the sole public transit company for Bucharest and its suburbs.
TransportMainText4: By 1939 Little Paris had a modern fleet of hundreds of buses and trams bought from big producers or built locally, and a well developed network of routes that covered the city and its metropolitan area.
RoyalMainText1: From 1866 to 1947 Romania was ruled by the Romanian Royal Family. The first king of Romania, Carol I of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, came to Bucharest in 1866 and ruled the country until 1881 as a 'Domnitor', without the official title of King. On the 10th of May 1881 Romania became a Kingdom, with Carol I as its first king.
RoyalMainText2: King Carol I had the longest rule of any Romanian leader, for 48 years (from 1866 to 1914), and took Romania from a backwater state to a modern and industrializing country. Without a male heir, Carol I was succeeded by his nephew King Ferdinand I.
RoyalMainText3: King Ferdinand, although of Prussian origin and a cousin to the German Kaiser Wilhelm II, chose to put Romania's interests before his own family ties, by joining the Entente in World War I.
RoyalMainText4: With both public opinion and the government being staunchly francophile, and Romanians both in the Kingdom and in neighbouring empires wanting unify, Ferdinand gained the title of 'the Loyal One', by entering the Great War against his own country of origin, in order to achieve the ideal of a unified Greater Romania.
RoyalMainText5: King Ferdinand I ruled from 1914 to 1927, being the King that unified all Romanians, gave voting rights to the masses, gave lands to the peasantry and signed a new modern constitution in 1923.
RoyalMainText6: After King Ferdinand's death, due to problems in the Romanian Royal Family regarding the heir, Carol II, Michael I became King at the very early age of 6 years old, being under the watch of regency council.
RoyalMainText7: After some internal political events, Carol II returned to Romania from exile and took the throne in 1930. A controversial figure both today and in the period, he is mostly remembered today as a corrupt individual, who favored life's pleasures more than the country's affairs. Yet, he also had his merits. He invested heavily in culture and education and wanted to modernise Romania.
RoyalMainText8: However, King Carol II's most infamous act was the capitulation of three of Romania's historical regions (Bessarabia, Northern Transylvania and Southern Dobrogea), the most important being Bessarabia. This led to his abdication and the country's further fall into totalitarianism under the rule of Army Marshall Ion Antonescu.
RoyalMainText9: After his father's abdication, King Michael I regained the throne at the age of 19, starting his second period of rule in 1940. Unfortunately, the young Michael was not allowed to rule the country proper, being forced into the shadow of Marshall Antonescu.
RoyalMainText10: King Michael tried to the best of his abilities to lead Romania through the Second World War and its aftermath, being the decisive factor in Romania's withdrawal from the Axis in 1944 and the coup against Ion Antonescu, that shortened the war by at least 6 months according to most historians.
RoyalMainText11: Unfortunately, after World War II, history was not kind to Romania and its Royal Family. As the Iron Curtain descended upon Eastern Europe, Stalin's communists forced King Michael to abdicate in 1947. After three years of opposition against the forced soviet occupation and communist influence, the King was pushed into signing the abdication at gunpoint and under the threat that 1000 students, that supported the monarchy, would be executed.
UniformsMainText1: During World War I, Romania had uniforms that very closely resembled those of the French Army. After The Great War, Romania adopted a more earth brown color, a kaki inspired by the British Army. The Military's look started, from the 1920s onwards, to shift towards earth tones and a British style of dress.
UniformsMainText2: What remained consistent however, up until World War II, was the King's insignia on the helmet of soldiers and the crown as a symbol for each uniform.
